chapters.label: 01 Purpose
chapters.title: Purpose
chapters.instruction: Learn what Oath & Action does, and how its pillars and nonpartisan rules shape every piece.
intro: Oath & Action is a nonpartisan publication and a set of tools for people in every state who live under public rules they rarely get to read. Our mission is “Help people understand and improve the rules that shape their lives.”

The ampersand in our name is the hinge, the joint a door swings on. It joins a promise to the action that keeps it, so every piece explains and tracks a decision, then turns to the people who make it and the step a reader can take. Chapter 04 draws the hinge and sets its rules.

rules.title: Keep red off every party, side and person.
Draw every party in one neutral ink, with its name on the mark.
Run a two-way scale from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.
On Prussian, turn identity marks White and data marks Newsprint.
Color a map by the rule or measure the story covers.
Show domes, columns and flags only in a captioned photograph of that place.
Keep party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear and protest slogans out of brand graphics.
Photograph people doing public work, and caption who, what, where and when.
Draw no more than one example in four from one atlas domain, or one in five from one state.
Rotate examples across levels of government and regions.
When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.
Log each example’s domain, state, region, level and backing coalition.
Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.
Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.
Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.
Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.
Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.
Set both halves of a hinge headline in one color and weight, and give the red to the ampersand.
Join people through a rule or place they share, and rotate their order.
Name parties, the left or the right in a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.
Open every kicker with one content label.
In a process piece, name the step and leave the side to the reader.
Put a position piece’s label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.
Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.

chapters.label: 02 Voice
chapters.title: Voice
chapters.instruction: Write the way you’d explain a rule to a neighbor, and quote the brand lines exactly.
intro: Our tagline is “A country that answers to its people.” People can hold an office to account once they know which office decided. So we name who acts, in words you would use at a kitchen table, as in “A regulator or a board approves your rate.”

Our reader promise is “We explain how a decision is made and give you a practical way to take part.” A reader can take part only in a decision they can follow, which is why clarity comes first in our editorial commitment, “Clarity is our duty. Action is our promise.”

chapters.label: 03 Identity
chapters.title: Identity
chapters.instruction: Pick the lockup that fits the surface and size, and give it room on every side.
intro: The wordmark is our name drawn as one piece of artwork: OATH and ACTION in heavy capitals, joined by ampersand B, the red ampersand we drew for Oath & Action. A lockup is a fixed arrangement of the wordmark with another part, such as the tagline or the lockmark, the 3 by 3 grid of nodes that chapter 08 explains.

Every mark here is a vector master drawn for a range of sizes. You place the master, color it with tokens and leave room around it. In this chapter x means the height of the wordmark’s capitals, and the pages show today’s wordmark width. The condensed width, which Dustin Cathcart is weighing, appears only in the wordmark width proofs after chapter 08.

rules.title: Place the wordmark from its master file.
Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.
Keep one cap height of clear space on every side.
Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.
Set the marks in their colors on the four approved surfaces.
Use L3 for the masthead, and drop the lockmark when the bar gets narrow.
Use L8 as the one monogram, and retire the spaced “O & A”.
Join a partner with a hairline, and keep our ampersand inside our name.

chapters.label: 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
chapters.title: The Ampersand and the hinge
chapters.instruction: Use the ampersand once per composition to join a commitment to what it produces.
intro: The ampersand is the hinge of the brand. It joins an oath, the commitment a person or an office makes, to the action that keeps it, and in our headlines it joins a rule to its result. Ampersand B is our own drawing: one pen path that crosses itself at the waist, with a beak at the top right and a tail that lands on the baseline.

This chapter covers B drawn alone and the four places the hinge appears: the hinge headline, the hinge divider, the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge. It ends with the tiles for avatars and the app icon, and the large crop for covers.

rules.title: Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.
Give each composition one ampersand moment.
Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.
Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.
Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.
Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.
Put B on a Charcoal tile for avatars and the app icon.
Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.

chapters.label: 05 Color
chapters.title: Color
chapters.instruction: Choose a surface first, then the text and graphic colors that pass on it.
intro: Oath & Action works in seven colors, and each one has a job. Newsprint, a warm off-white, is the page most of our work sits on, and Charcoal carries the words. Pillar Red marks the one thing a reader should see first in each view, meaning each screen, card, slide or printed page. The other four do narrower work: Prussian, our dark blue, holds panels of dates and figures, Stone draws hairlines, Verdigris, a muted green, shows success and focus, and White serves specimens and email.

Every pair in this chapter carries a contrast ratio, a measure of how far apart two colors sit in lightness. It runs from 1 to 1 for the same color up to 21 to 1 for black on white, by the formula in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). We measured each ratio on the token values, the exact colors our code names. Pick the surface first, and the tables tell you which text and marks can sit on it.

rules.title: Cover most of every view in Newsprint.
Set text only on color pairs that pass.
Give each view one working red.
Show every state with a word or a shape as well as a color.
Keep marks that carry meaning at 3 to 1, and give red on Newsprint a Charcoal keyline.
Give each tint one named job, and keep tints off identity marks.
Set charts and the atlas on Newsprint, in the chart palette.

chapters.label: 06 Type
chapters.title: Type
chapters.instruction: Set every word at a readable size with the three faces and the type scale.
intro: Three typefaces carry every word we publish: Inter Tight for headlines and big figures, Inter for reading and the interface, and Lora Italic for the words we quote. Each has a single job, so a reader can tell a headline from a quotation before reading either.

We set sizes in rem, a unit tied to the reader’s own text setting, which is 16 px unless they change it. A reader who enlarges text gets larger type everywhere, and no text on screen sets below 13 px.

rules.title: Keep each typeface to its one job.
Take every size from the type scale.
Set no text on screen below 13 px.
Tighten tracking only as headings grow.
Line up figures in tables, and give negatives the true minus sign.
Balance a heading’s lines, and keep two words or more on its last line.
Hang opening quotation marks outside the text edge.
Set body text at 60 to 75 characters a line.
Set email type in the system font stack.
Load the three faces, and let no other face stand in.

chapters.label: 07 Layout and spacing
chapters.title: Layout and spacing
chapters.instruction: Build each page on the column grid and spacing scale, readable at every width.
intro: Every page sits on a column grid and spaces its parts in steps of 8 px. The grid changes at set window widths, called breakpoints, from 12 columns on a desktop to four on a phone, and each paragraph spans the columns that keep its lines at the measure chapter 06 sets.
A page also has to read at 320 px wide, and with its text at twice the size, with nothing cut off and no scrolling sideways.

rules.title: Space everything in steps of the 8 px scale.
Set each page on the column grid for its width.
Span body text across the columns that hold its measure.
Set a heading closer to the text it introduces than to the block above.
Set breakpoints in em, so larger text gets fewer columns.
Make every page read at 320 px wide, with nothing lost.

chapters.label: 08 The Signal Grid
chapters.title: The Signal Grid
chapters.instruction: Keep the lockmark to its fixed places, and put a key beside every Signal Grid that codes content.
intro: Democracy has a structure. The lockmark draws it as nine nodes joined by links, with the lever, a larger red node at bottom right, at the place where one change moves the rest. It sits beside the wordmark in the masthead and in a few fixed places, and its drawing never changes.

The Signal Grid uses the same nine nodes to code one thing about a piece: how far a bill has moved, which recurring series it belongs to, or which pillar it serves. A coded grid always sits beside words that say what it shows.

rules.title: Draw the lockmark from its master for its size, and keep its drawing fixed.
Place the lockmark only in its fixed positions and sizes.
Set a key beside every Signal Grid that codes content.
Let each grid code one thing, chosen in this order: tracker progress, a series route, a pillar corner.
Show tracker progress with a shape for each stage, from 40 px.
Give each recurring series one fixed route that ends on its pillar’s corner.
Light one corner to name a pillar, and print the pillar’s name beside it.
Build the kicker from a 24 px grid, a 24 px icon and a label.
Keep every grid state still, and say it in words.

proofs.title: Wordmark width proofs
proofs.instruction: Compare each piece at both wordmark widths at actual size, so Dustin can choose one.
intro: Dustin Cathcart, our founder and editor, chooses the wordmark’s width from these proofs. Each proof shows one piece at actual size at today’s width and at the condensed width, both with ampersand B, set on one edge or one line so the wordmark is the one thing that changes. Today’s width stays in use until he chooses.
We recommend today’s width. At the same height the condensed drawing only runs narrower, and its heavy capitals sit close to the lettering of campaign signs. Its monogram also reads as 0&A.

groups.alt: The wordmark at both widths side by side at true size, today’s width at left and the condensed width at right, each at the same height so the difference shows as width: from the 16 pixel masters, 152 against 120 pixels wide; from the 24 pixel masters, 221 against 181; from the display masters at 48 pixels tall, 435 against 342. Below them, the stacked lockup and the O & A monogram at both widths.

Today’s wordmark runs 221 pixels and the condensed one 181, so the condensed lockmark sits 40 pixels further left. Below them, the two 390 pixel phone bars with the wordmark and a menu button, also on one left edge.

notes: The monogram, L8, on the Charcoal tile that Rule 04.7 sets as the default, in a circle and a square. A feed draws an avatar at about 32 to 48 px, where L8 at either width sets its capitals under the 14 px floor. Rule 04.7’s avatar, ampersand B alone, reads at that size and is the same at both widths, so we recommend it whichever width Dustin chooses.

Today’s capitals stand 41, 20 and 10 pixels tall; the condensed capitals stand 50, 24 and 12, and its narrow O reads close to a zero. At 48 pixels both fall under the 14 pixel floor.

title.text: A country that answers to its people.

h3.text: Rule 01.1 Keep red off every party, side and person.
